title: Patrick
hookLine: a British boy kidnapped to Ireland escapes, then goes back to the people who enslaved him

cards: Raiders come to a family's land in Britain and carry off a boy, along with many others, across the sea to Ireland. He's put to work watching animals on the hills, alone.
His father was a deacon, his grandfather a priest, and the boy, by his own account, had paid none of it much attention. Now, out on the hillside, he starts to pray.
Years later he'll write the story himself, in rough Latin he apologizes for.

teach.b: Patrick's Confession doesn't read like a legend. It reads like a man explaining his life to people who doubted him. On that hillside, he says, the love of God grew in him.
He prayed day and night, in snow and frost and rain, and felt no harm. Then one night he heard a voice in his sleep: your ship is ready.
He ran a long way to a coast he didn't know, talked his way onto a ship, and after hard days, and some years, was home with his family. They begged him never to leave again. Then came another dream.
A man named Victoricus seemed to come from Ireland, carrying letters, more than could be counted.
He handed one over, and at the top it said: The Voice of the Irish.

teach.h: BACK TO THE PEOPLE WHO TOOK HIM.
teach.b: As he read, he heard the people beside the western sea calling, as if with one voice: holy boy, we beg you, come and walk among us again.

teach.h: NO SHAMROCK: A MAN WHO WENT BACK.
teach.b: And he went back. To the land where he'd been a slave, to the people who had taken him.

As a bishop he baptized and ordained, and refused gifts, even handing back what was left on the altar, so no one could say he'd come for profit. It wasn't safe: he writes of being seized and put in chains.
Jesus had said, in the King James: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." Patrick doesn't cast himself as the hero.
He calls himself a sinner, the least of the faithful, and gives the credit to God. The shamrock and the snakes come from later stories. His own pages hold something stranger: a man who went back.

how: Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox and other Christians honor Patrick as a saint and the apostle of Ireland; his Confession is read as his own account of his captivity, escape and return.

o: a Roman soldier who brought the faith to Britain
an Irish king who first sent monks to Rome
a freed captive who went back to Ireland as a bishop

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the voice that sent him home
come and walk among us again

s: he came from Britain and was carried to Ireland as a captive.
the shamrock and the snakes come from Patrick's own writing
they come from later stories. his own pages tell of captivity, escape and going back.

games.q: you've escaped slavery and you're home. your family begs you never to leave. then you dream that the people who held you are calling you back. what do you do?
o: go back, to the people who enslaved you.
send someone else in your place.
games.why: Patrick went back to Ireland as a bishop, to the people who had taken him, and he wasn't always safe there.

practice: Let a place or person tied to an old hurt come to mind, not the deepest, something you can hold today; going back in your heart never means walking back into harm.
Is there a good thing you could bring there now, a kind word, or simply wishing them well from a distance? If you pray, bring that place to God; if not, hold it in steady goodwill.

wordCard.voice: Patrick. The captive who escaped, then heard the voice of the Irish and went back. That ends a week of Jerome, the pears, Ostia, Rome, the golden mouth and Chalcedon.

orig.note: Latin, from Patrick's own Confession: the voice of the Irish, the words at the top of the letter in his dream.

carryVoice: Your line: the voice of the irish. He went back, carrying something good. A week done.
